newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds still depressed by Greenspan, dollar weak.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds still depressed by Greenspan, dollar weak.

text.p: Stocks and bonds fell Thursday as Wall Street remained unnerved a day after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned that stock prices might be too high and hinted that the central bank may raise interest rates.
The dollar fell sharply against the yen, which was boosted by a report of unexpected strength in the Japanese economy.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 58.11 points, or 0.83 percent, at 6,925.07, for a two-day loss of more than 100 points.

But the Dow's stiff losses paled in comparison to the technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index's fall of 27.89 points, or more than 2 percent, to 1,312.66. It was the steepest one-day decline on Nasdaq since last July 23's drop of 32.32 points.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,601 to 896 on active volume of 464 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Rising interest rates in the bond market again posed a problem for stocks.

The closely watched 30-year Treasury bond was off 13/32, which raised its yield to 6.81 percent from Wednesday's close of 6.78 percent as jitters over Greenspan's blunt comments on interest rates pressed on the bond market.
The heightened sense of caution in the stock market was felt most heavily in the technology arena, where investors were clearly rethinking the group's price levels.

"There is a fundamental valuation change occurring," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "The communications equipment makers in particular are being revalued and the valuations are going down."

The selling pressure on technology stocks -- a group that has performed unimpressively in recent weeks -- appeared to reach a flashpoint with news late Wednesday of the merger between network equipment makers U.S. Robotics Corp. and 3Com Corp.
Opinions on Wall Street about the $6.6 billion merger varied but most telling for the networking group, some analysts said, was what they described as the low price 3Com is paying for U.S. Robotics.

"If anything, this deal is more of a take-under than a takeover," said Salomon Brothers analyst Peter Swartz. "This deal says the days of the 35 to 40 percent premiums paid in previous networking acquisitions are over."

The dollar fell to its lowest level against the yen in a month. After rising by roughly nine yen -- over 7 percent -- in the first six weeks of the year to a four-year high of 124.82 on Feb. 14, the dollar has fallen more than four yen in the last two weeks.
The dollar stood at 120.67 yen late in New York, down from 122.06 late Wednesday. Against the German mark, the dollar slid to 1.6880 from 1.6896 late Wednesday.
Precious metals prices rose, led by platinum and palladium amid threats of a strike at a giant Russian mine.
April platinum at the New York Mercantile Exchange closed up $9.60 an ounce at $396.30 after setting a four-month high at $399.80. June palladium closed up $7.20 an ounce at $157.45.
Oil prices closed mostly lower, with April crude oil on the Nymex ending down 22 cents a barrel at $20.89 and March heating oil down 0.65 cent a gallon at 56.03 cents.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed 9.9 points higher at 4,339.2. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average edged back above the 19,000 level to finish 30.64 points, or 0.16 percent, higher at 19,021.56.
